content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to reduce the pre-training overhead of Masked AutoEncoder (MAE), by applying higher masking ratio (95%) as well as reducing pre-training epochs and decoder depth. Meanwhile at the fine-tunning phase, the authors change the hyper-parameter of layer-wise learning rate decay to increase the finetune accuracy. The authors have conducted experiments with ViT-Base and -Small to demonstrate the efficacy in terms of the top-1 fine-tune accuracy on ImageNet1K.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The proposed speedup techniques are kind of trivial. 

+ Reducing the pre-training epoch from 1600 to 100: Since every epoch endures nearly the same time, this manner undoubtedly has 16x speedup. 

+ Reducing the decoder depth from 8 to 1: since every layer (or block) of the decoder has the same architecture, this manner undoubtedly has 8x speedup for the decoding. 

+ Increasing the mask ratio from 75% to 90%, this manner also undoubtedly accelerates the encoding.

Overall, the proposed techniques are not insightful or novel ways to reduce the pre-training overhead. Everyone plays with MAE might have tried these small games.
***
There is no doubt that, as also recognized by the authors, such models pre-trained with extremely less epoch, model capacity and visible tokens will have poor transferability than the original MAE. To this end, the authors find that increasing the layer-wise learning rate decay (LLRD) at the fine-tuning phase can significantly mitigate the performance loss.

However, the reviewer has some concerns about the authors’ evaluation: 

+ In most of the current practices, the pre-training and downstream transfer are decoupled. Once the pre-trained model is obtained, it will serve as the starting point for many downstream tasks. To this end, the authors cannot rely on adjusting a recipe of one specific downstream task to draw the conclusion that the transferability of the new pre-trained model is maintained. 

+ The reviewer conjectures that adjusting the LLRD will not benefit downstream tasks with dense prediction such segmentation and detection. To this end, the pre-trained model with extremely less epoch, model capacity and visible tokens is still a poorer starting point that is not deployable. 

+ How about using this new finetune recipe for the original MAE?
***
There are some other issues should be addressed.

+ The reviewer has run MAE as well as other MIM variants for many times using V100 and A100, however, he has never tried on the A5000 used in this paper. Does the experiments in this paper device-independent?

+ The authors claim in the introduction that, “This heavy pre-training cost may potentially limit the wider explorations of MIM in the large-computation regime (e.g., larger models)”. 
However, the reviewer does not find such evidence in the experiments to echo this ambition. Currently, all the experiments are conducted with relatively small models (-base and -small). Can the authors compare their methods with the ViT-Large, which is the standard variant that the original MAE uses. According to the experience of the reviewer, the performance will drop at this case.

+ “a asymmetric” => “an asymmetric” 

+ “may potentially limits” => “may potentially limit”

+ “can still produces” => “can still produce”

+ duplicate and wrong reference for “Generate pretraining from pixels”

+ duplicate and wrong reference for “An image is worth 16x16 words: Transformers for image recognition at scale”

+ missing paper title for the reference with authors “Elad Hoffer, …”

+ In the subsection “masked image modeling” of the related works, in fact, SimMIM does not use a 75% masking ratio.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well-written and easy to follow since the main message of the paper is very simple. 

However, the novelty of the proposed speedup techniques is very limited. Reducing the epoch, decoder depth and increasing the masking ratio are all very common practices. 

Since the authors conduct their experiments on A5000 and the reviewer is more familiar with using V100 to train MAE, the reviewer cannot figure out whether the current results can be fully reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper proposes to speed up the pre-training of MAE by reducing the training epochs, decoder depth and increasing the masking ratio. To mitigate the performance drop of the pre-trained model, the authors find that enlarging the layer-wise learning rate decay will benefit a specific downstream task, i.e., global image classification. 

From the perspective of the reviewer, the main message of this paper is not very novel to the community since the proposed techniques are all very common practices. 

Moreover, the evaluation of the downstream transfer is problematic and the reviewer has raised his concerns in the weakness part. 

Overall, the reviewer believes that this paper is currently under the bar to be accepted to ICLR.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper presents an engineering effort to make MAE pre-training fast using the ViT-base model.
The authors use short training epochs, a high masking ratio (90%), and a lightweight decoder (1-layer) during the pre-trining.
During the fine-tuning, the authors compensate the pre-matured weights due to the fast pre-training by adequately setting the layer-wise learning rate decay (LLRD) value. Based on the hyperparameter sweep, authors observe that using higher LLRD values, which is less conservative to update the weights, compared to the original finetuning recipe works well.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

*+*  The authors revealed the interesting fact that fast MAE pre-training is possible with proper fine-tuning recipes.

**Weakness**

*-* The experimental results are only conducted with the ViT-base model in the classification task. The main results must be verified in other model regimes (up/downward) and tasks (seg/det). Without these results, the authors cannot claim the current message strongly.

*-* Moreover, the authors should ablate the proposals in terms of fine-tuning accuracy and efficiency (FLOPs analysis). Currently, we need to identify which one makes the pre-training the fastest and most effective (or less effective): 1) short epoch, 2) high masking ratio, and 3) lightweight decoder. Also, what is their compounded effect?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**

The paper is easy to follow.

**Quality**

The paper needs several essential experiments. The authors are encouraged to try other model sizes and tasks. Moreover, thorough ablation studies are required.

**Novelty**

This paper does not target a novel technical contribution. Instead, it attempts to show that fast MAE pre-training is possible if a good fine-tuning recipe is provided.

**Reproducibility**

The authors provided the implementation details. The proposal is easy to be reproduced.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I appreciate the authors conducting good set of engineering to make MAE pre-training fast.
However, the main concern with this paper is lack of experimental validations.
The authors claim should be more strong if this found observation holds for other model sizes and tasks.
Moreover, the authors should provide thorough analysis on the learned representation quality and increased efficiency by shortening the pre-training epochs, increasing masking ratio, and making decoder lightweight.
Overall, I think the current paper needs further improvements to be accepted.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces the layer-wise decay learning rate schedule to reduce the epochs of MAE-pretraining. The authors find that layer-wise decay learning can accelerate the convergence of pretraining. The authors conduct experiments on ImageNet and find ME-pre training can converge well with only 100 epochs. And the authors extend the layer-wise decay learning method on SupMAE.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 

The phenomenon of using layer-wise learning rate decay on pretrained phase is surprising.

Weaknesses: 

Although the longer pretraining only has slight improvement on imageNet, it can learn better representation, and the pre-training model has better transferability on downstream tasks (e.g., object detection and segmentation), the authors don’t show the downstream experiments in the draft.

The layer-wise learning rate decay is a widely used technical method on transformers in the NLP community. One of my concerns is the technical novelty of this paper.

The pretraining and finetune phases have many hyperparameter differences with original MAE (e.g., decoder depth, ft learning rate schedule). It may lead the learning rate decay tricks to generalize to other models (e.g., vit-large, vit-huge, swim-transformer)

content.summary_of_the_paper:
1.	The paper accelerates MAE training significantly by adjusting the training recipe, including mask ratio, decoder depth, batch size and LLRD in fine-tuning stage.

2.	The finding can also generalize to other MAE extensions, such as SupMAE.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 

1.	This paper verifies that the vanilla MAE can be significantly accelerated by adjusting the recipe of both pre-training and fine-tuning. Specifically, LLRD of finetuning has a big impact on ImageNet fine-tuning Acc.

Weaknesses:

1.	The motivation could be clearer. As one pre-trained model can be fine-tuned on various downstream tasks. The contribution of reducing pre-training time cost is less significant considering the performance drop. 

2.	The modifications of pre-training recipe mainly focus on mask ratio, decoder depth, which are already studied in MAE paper. For example, a one-block decoder can already achieve good finetuning performance on ImageNet. Thus, the contribution of pre-training recipe is incremental.

3.	The findings about LLRD are quite interesting. However, will this generalize well to other downstream tasks like object detection? If not, the value of these findings is limited to one task. Besides, only ImageNet data is considered in this paper: ImageNet-1k, ImageNet-200, ImageNet-10%. Will the best LLRD on ImageNet generalize well to other data domain?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper has a clear clarification and is easy to reproduce, I believe. Yet I do have concerns about novelty.
content.summary_of_the_review: According to my listed concerns, I think the contribution of this paper is below the acceptance threshold. I’ll update my rating according to authors’ responses.
